title: U.S. tariffs on China were followed by larger relative import-price declines in emerging markets
bank: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
summary: Goods from China targeted by the 2018–19 U.S. tariffs became cheaper relative to comparison goods in markets outside the United States and China. By 2021 the estimated relative decline in average import unit values was 4.4% across the bystander-country sample. It was 4.8% for emerging markets and 2.2% for advanced economies. The authors contrast that evidence with U.S. imports, where they can reproduce the absence of an offsetting decline in prices charged by Chinese exporters in 2018 and 2019. An exporter losing access to a large market could thus lower prices in other destinations without reducing the pre-duty price charged to the U.S. buyer (figures 4–7 and appendix C.5).

Sofie Grouws, Sharon Jeon, Giulia Lo Forte and Justin Pierce compare annual UN Comtrade records at the level of exporter, importer and six-digit product for 2017–21. Relative changes are measured against a pre-tariff 2017 baseline. The analysis separates Chinese products that faced U.S. tariffs by 2021 from comparison flows, accounting for common product-year movements and persistent differences between trading partners. A change from reporting units to kilograms could otherwise create an entirely artificial price change. The authors reconcile primary and alternative quantity units where feasible. Price is the value divided by physical quantity within each trade flow. A move towards cheaper varieties within a product category can lower that measure even when an identical item’s transaction price does not change. A finer European product classification gives similar results (sections 2, 3 and 5).

The regional differences were sizable. For ASEAN economies, estimated relative prices fell about 12% in both 2020 and 2021. Emerging markets’ greater average decline need not mean that every consumer or importer paid less. The baseline gives each observed trade flow equal weight. An import-value-weighted result answers a different question about flows that matter most for total spending, and the paper reports less precise weighted estimates. The quantity of targeted Chinese products imported into bystander markets rose by an estimated 8% in 2019 relative to comparison goods. An extended sample shows that values and quantities of subsequently targeted goods were already trending upward before the tariffs. Their ratio exhibited no comparable pre-trend, leaving the price result on firmer ground than a causal interpretation of the volume increase (figures 8–10 and appendix C.4).

Larger price declines occurred where the United States had previously absorbed a large share of China’s exports of the product and where destination markets sourced imports from fewer suppliers. Markets with more concentrated sourcing could have had more room for margins to fall, although the study observes unit values rather than markups. Differences in geopolitical alignment also mattered. The authors use countries’ voting distance from China at the United Nations. Table 5 and the positive distance coefficient in figure 15 imply smaller relative price declines farther from China, consistent with the conclusion and country examples. One sentence in section 6.4 describes the direction oppositely. The estimates establish a relationship with alignment without identifying a commercial or political decision by an individual exporter.

Cheaper imported goods could benefit buyers or downstream producers while creating pressure for local competitors. The paper estimates border-price relationships, leaving retail pass-through, domestic margins and welfare as open questions. The authors also caution against mechanically applying the estimates to tariffs imposed in 2025–26, whose scale and country coverage differed from those of the historical episode.

questions.question: Which import-price declines reached purchasers in the industries or countries of interest?
questions.detail: The paper measures average values at the border and shows larger changes for some emerging markets. Consult destination-country customs microdata, producer price components, retailer price records and company filings on sourcing costs. Match like products and distinguish final goods from intermediate inputs. This would test whether gains accrued to households, importing firms or distributors and whether domestic competitors faced pressure on their margins.

questions.question: How much of the decline reflects discounted varieties versus a shift to cheaper models?
questions.detail: Harmonizing units removes spurious conversions and the more detailed European check is reassuring. Quality and exporter composition can still change within product codes, particularly outside Europe. Examine repeated exporter-product transactions, invoice prices, model descriptions and physical units in customs declarations. A change in matched-item prices would imply a different shock to incumbent suppliers and to inflation forecasts than substitution towards lower-priced products.

questions.question: Which features of the historical tariff episode would survive a change in country coverage?
questions.detail: Price effects varied with prior exposure, supplier concentration and geopolitical proximity, while the newer tariffs covered a wider range of countries. Start with official tariff schedules and pre-policy bilateral customs shares, then map competing suppliers, exemptions and tariff dates. Compare product-destination exposures before using the old coefficient. The exercise would identify where an investment forecast relies on an actual alternative market remaining open.
